title: Risk of Autistic Spectrum Disorder in Subgroups of a Multi‐Ethnic Population in the United Kingdom‐A Case Control Study
content: Background: A previous multinational epidemiological study showed that in countries where assortative mating dominates autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence is higher compared to countries with predominantly arranged marriages. We set as objective to investigate whether this association is reproducible in the multi-ethnic population of a single setting with defined socioeconomic environment and whether it is due to confounding factors known to be associated with ASD. Methods: In a retrospective case control study all children born within a 2 year period and formally diagnosed with ASD were compared to children born within the same day in the same hospital without a later diagnosis of ASD. Factors influenced by nutrition in pregnancy, maternal metabolic syndrome or adverse pregnancy outcome, gender and grouping according to parental ethnic origin were compared between children with and without ASD. Results: A total of 353 children with a diagnosis of ASD were compared with 2103 controls. Children with ASD were significantly more likely to be male with an odds ratio of 3.1 (95% CI 2.4 to 4.1). There was no difference in percentage being born prematurely, birthweight or head circumference. Amongst children with ASD Caucasian children were underrepresented and children with parents from Bangladesh or Pakistan over-represented compared to controls born on the same day. Children with parents from India, African ancestry, other Asian countries, or mixed ethnic backgrounds were represented in proportions consistent with the control group. Conclusions: Male gender and parental origin from Bangladesh or Pakistan were associated with an increased odds of autism spectrum disorder in a multi-ethnic population in the UK.
